quarters:Santa Maria and the upper town.name: Santa Maria and the upper town
quarters:Santa Maria and the upper town.teaser: Lanes paved with slate stood on edge, climbing to a white church that watches the whole bay
quarters:Santa Maria and the upper town.story: Leave the front by any alley and the ground changes under your feet. The upper town is paved in rastell: slabs of local slate set on edge in tight rows, so that storm water runs down the joints instead of tearing up the street. The lanes are barely three or four metres wide, whitewash close on both sides, doors and shutters painted, bougainvillea over the lintels. They wind uphill to the terrace of Santa Maria, where the roofs fall away below you and the bay opens out towards the cape. Walk it early, before the day visitors, when the loudest thing in the lane is a broom on slate.
quarters:Santa Maria and the upper town.why: Climb to the church terrace for the whole bay laid out under the roofs, then come down by a different lane.
facts: The rastell lanes, the whitewash and the doorways between the front and the church
Early morning, or the last hour of daylight on the church terrace; the lanes stay cooler than the front in any month
The terrace in front of Santa Maria (the church has its own card); wear shoes with grip, as the slate turns slick when wet
Casa Anita on Carrer Miquel Rosset, by the church; Es Balconet on Carrer Sant Antoni; Es Bar de Dalt's olive-tree terrace above the old town (all in the tables; check autumn opening)
quarters:Santa Maria and the upper town.maps_query: Església de Santa Maria, Cadaqués, Girona, Spain

quarters:Sa Riba and Es Portitxó.name: Sa Riba and Es Portitxó
quarters:Sa Riba and Es Portitxó.teaser: The one house in town that refused the whitewash, and the little square where the sardana is danced
quarters:Sa Riba and Es Portitxó.story: Sa Riba is the front where the old town meets the water, its houses rising out of the sea wall. Among them stands the one that breaks the rule of white: Casa Serinyana, called Casa Blaua, built in 1913 by the architect Salvador Sellés for a doctor, Octavi Serinyana, with a tower at each end and doors and windows framed in sky-blue glazed tile. It is a private house, seen from the street. A few steps on, Es Portitxó, the small square at the old port gate, is where the village gathers; on feast days the cobla plays there and the circles of the sardana form on the paving.
quarters:Sa Riba and Es Portitxó.why: Look up at Casa Blaua's blue tile from the waterline, then take a coffee on the Portitxó and watch the village pass.
facts: The sea-wall houses of the front, Casa Serinyana's blue tile and the Portitxó square
Morning light on the facades; early evening on the square, when the village comes out
Casa Serinyana (private, seen from outside only); a feast day with sardanes on the square
Casa Nun on Plaça des Portitxó; Es Trull on Carrer Portitxó; Es Baluard, built into the sea wall on Riba Nemesi Llorens, open in high season only (all in the tables)

quarters:La Riera.name: La Riera
quarters:La Riera.teaser: A riverbed with no river: it floods only in storms and carries the cars and the Monday market instead
quarters:La Riera.story: The Riera de Sant Vicenç is a torrent bed that comes down through the middle of the village to the bay, and it is dry almost all year. It earns its name only in a cloudburst, when water off the hills runs down it fast. The rest of the time its flat floor does the work a valley bottom does in any hill town: it is the road in, the main line of parking and, on Mondays, the market (the larder card 'The Monday market on the Riera' has the stalls and the hours). It splits the village, and every walk crosses it. Compartir's address is on it.
quarters:La Riera.why: Leave the car here, then come back on a Monday morning for the market instead of the parking.
facts: The way in, the parking and the Monday market
Monday morning for the market; on other days it is where you arrive and leave
The Monday market (its own card in the larder)
Compartir, Riera de Sant Vicenç s/n (in the tables; book ahead)

quarters:Es Poal.name: Es Poal
quarters:Es Poal.teaser: Stand on the pebbles where a teenage Dalí set his easel, and line the bay up with his 1920 canvas
quarters:Es Poal.story: Es Poal is one of the small pebble shores strung along the bay, where boats are still hauled up on the stones. In 1920, aged about sixteen and still painting in an impressionist hand, Salvador Dalí set up here for 'View of Cadaqués from Playa Poal': the white village across the water, the church on its hump, boats in the foreground. Stand on the beach and the composition is still in front of you. Around it the promenade does what it always did at this end of the front: terraces, ice cream, the aperitif while the boats come in. It is free, and every walk along the bay passes it.
quarters:Es Poal.why: Pull the painting up on your phone and match it to the real view from the stones.
facts: Boats on the pebbles, the white village across the water and the evening terraces
Late afternoon into the aperitif hour
The view Dalí painted in 1920; the boats drawn up on the shore
Talla on Riba Pitxot and Compartir on the Riera, both a short walk along the front (in the tables; Talla closes roughly November to March)

quarters:Es Llané.name: Es Llané
quarters:Es Llané.teaser: Two flat-rock beaches five minutes south, where the Dalí family spent its summers before Portlligat
quarters:Es Llané.story: Walk five minutes south of the centre and the town loosens into Es Llané: two urban beaches, Gran and Petit, of pebbles and flat schist ledges you can stretch out on. Llané Gran is a strip of roughly 130 by 12 metres. Behind this shore was the Dalí family's summer house, the one the young painter set behind his father in 'Portrait of my father and the house at Es Llaner' (1920). The boy spent his summers here long before Portlligat, and Federico García Lorca stayed in the house at Easter 1925; the colony card tells the rest. This is simply where to swim off the rocks.
quarters:Es Llané.why: Swim from the flat rocks early, while the water is still and the beach belongs to the village.
facts: Flat rocks to swim from, five minutes on foot from the centre, and the shore of the Dalí family's summers
Morning, before the beach fills; in mid-October the water is cooling, so pick a calm, sunny day
The shore and houses shown in Dalí's 1920 portrait of his father
No table of this guide on the beach itself: walk back to S'Estrop or Can Rafa on the central front (in the tables)

quarters:Portlligat.name: Portlligat
quarters:Portlligat.teaser: Over the hill from town, a closed cove of moored boats, a few white houses and a very still evening
quarters:Portlligat.story: Take the road over the rise north of the village and in about 1.2 km Cadaqués is gone. Portlligat is a small, nearly closed bay with an island across its mouth, fishing boats moored in the shallows and a handful of whitewashed houses along the shingle. Dalí lived here for half a century; his house has its own card, and so does the beach. What is left for this one is the hamlet itself: nets and boats, the walk over and back, and the end of the day, when the wind drops, the bay goes flat and the boats sit on their own reflections.
quarters:Portlligat.why: Walk over in the late afternoon, sit by the boats as the bay stills, and walk back to town for dinner.
facts: The moored fishing boats, the closed little bay, the walk over from town and the evening light
The Casa-Museu Dalí (timed tickets only) and Portlligat beach, each with its own card
No table of this guide in Portlligat: walk back over the hill to Talla on Riba Pitxot or Compartir on the Riera (in the tables)

curiosities:The rock older than shells.name: The rock older than shells
curiosities:The rock older than shells.teaser: The cape's schist was laid down as the first shelled animals appeared, then folded as continents collided
curiosities:The rock older than shells.story: The grey rock under Cadaqués began as mud on an ancient sea floor some 580 to 540 million years ago, around the time the first animals with hard shells were appearing. Then it was crushed, folded and partly melted in the Variscan collision of continents, roughly 300 million years ago. That heat drove white pegmatite veins through the dark mica-schist: the pale stripes you see in every cove of the cape. The tramuntana has been carving the folds ever since. Geologists come from all over to read this coast, and since 1998 it has been protected, land and sea, as the Parc Natural de Cap de Creus.
curiosities:The rock older than shells.why: Put your hand on a white pegmatite stripe in the dark rock: that is a 300-million-year-old crack filled with crystal.
facts: The white pegmatite veins in the grey schist at any cove of the cape; the Espai Cap de Creus at the lighthouse explains what you are looking at (its own card)

The old guide dates the folding to 310-280 million years ago in one place and 'some 300' in another; 'older than shells' is a round claim that holds only for the older end of the 580-540 million-year range, since shelled animals spread from about 540 million years ago. The park's area (13,886 ha, from Viquipèdia) was not re-checked

sources.label: Parcs Naturals de Catalunya — Parc Natural de Cap de Creus

curiosities:The tramuntana.name: The tramuntana
curiosities:The tramuntana.teaser: The north wind built the town: houses turn their backs to it, and it scrubs the sky clear as glass
curiosities:The tramuntana.story: The tramuntana is the cold, dry north wind that pours off the Pyrenees and down across the Empordà, and Cap de Creus, the last spur of the range, takes it head on. It can blow for days, hardest in winter and early spring. It shaped the town: low houses with thick walls, limewashed white, turning blank backs to the north. It shaped the cape, scouring the rock into the forms Dalí painted. And it makes the light. When the tramuntana has blown the haze out to sea, the air turns so clear that the far shore of the gulf seems close enough to swim to.
curiosities:The tramuntana.why: On a north-wind day, skip the boat and climb high: the clearest light of the year is the wind's doing.
facts: Mid-October is the start of its season: on a tramuntana day, stand on the church terrace or at the cape and watch the sea go white offshore under a clean sky (boat days are the warning card's business)

Guides say it 'gusts past 100 km/h' here. Meteocat warnings for the Alt Empordà do announce gusts above 100 km/h (March 2026), and Portbou, up the coast, logged about 120 km/h in a February 2026 storm, but no published record figure for Cap de Creus itself was found

curiosities:Parlar salat.name: Parlar salat
curiosities:Parlar salat.teaser: Here the beach is 'sa platja': the salted article of the Balearics survives at the end of the cape
curiosities:Parlar salat.story: Listen on the quay and in the shops and you may catch it: es instead of el, sa instead of la. This is the 'salted' article, built from the Latin ipse where standard Catalan took ille. Medieval texts show it across much of Catalonia; on the mainland it retreated almost everywhere, and today it is above all the article of the Balearic Islands. Cadaqués, reachable for centuries mainly by sea, held on to it, and it is written all over the map: Sa Riba, Es Poal, Es Llané, Sa Conca, Es Portitxó. The place names keep it even where everyday speech has moved on.
curiosities:Parlar salat.why: Read the names of the beaches and streets aloud: you are speaking the village's own Catalan.
facts: The beach and street names (Sa Riba, Es Poal, Es Llané, Sa Conca), and the talk at the Monday market

The old guide called Cadaqués the only mainland town where salat is everyday speech. Not so: Tàrbena and the Vall de Gallinera, inland Alicante villages resettled from Mallorca after 1610, kept it too, and Tàrbena holds a festival for it. Within Catalonia, Cadaqués is the best-known survival; no source found measures how many villagers still use it daily

curiosities:The monks bought the fish.name: The monks bought the fish
curiosities:The monks bought the fish.teaser: In 1030 the abbey on the mountain bought its rights here, and for centuries the bay fed the monks
curiosities:The monks bought the fish.story: Cadaqués enters the written record as property. A donation of 974 names it, and in 1030 the abbot of Sant Pere de Rodes, the Benedictine monastery high on the Verdera ridge across the peninsula, bought rights over the place from the counts of Roussillon, sharing the lordship with the counts of Empúries. In the reading the old guide gives, those were rights to the fisheries and ports, and the bay's catch went up the mountain to the monks' table for centuries. The monastery visit is the Sant Pere de Rodes card's; here it is enough to know that the fish on your plate once had an abbot for a landlord.
curiosities:The monks bought the fish.why: Order the day's fish from the bay and think of the thousand-year-old deed behind it.
facts: The day's catch at any table in the guide; the monastery itself is a day trip with its own card

A tourism history says the 1030 purchase was of rights over the place, bought from the counts of Roussillon and shared with the counts of Empúries; the old guide says rights to its fisheries and ports. The 974 donation comes from the old guide only and was not re-checked

sources.label: Fascinating Spain — Cadaqués and Portlligat (history)

curiosities:Burned in 1444, sacked by Ba.name: Burned in 1444, sacked in 1543
curiosities:Burned in 1444, sacked by Ba.teaser: Raiders burned the town and its records in 1444; a century later Barbarossa's fleet came for the church
curiosities:Burned in 1444, sacked by Ba.story: A town at the tip of a peninsula, with no garrison and a good harbour, was an easy mark. A document in the municipal archive records that in 1444 raiding galleys set Cadaqués on fire and burned its papers, one reason so little of its medieval past is written down. In 1543 it happened again: a fleet of some twenty-five ships under the corsair Barbarossa put the town to the torch, and the parish church of Santa Maria burned with much of the village. Cadaqués rebuilt its walls, and on the same site raised the larger church you climb to today, whose story is the Santa Maria card's.
curiosities:Burned in 1444, sacked by Ba.why: Stand at Santa Maria knowing it is the church that rose from the 1543 ashes.
facts: Climb to Santa Maria, the rebuilding that followed 1543 (its own card)

The old guide says 'Moorish galleys' burned the town in 1444, citing the municipal archive; a tourism history just says it was burned. For 1543, tourism histories name Barbarossa's fleet of 25 ships, while an article in the Annals de l'Institut d'Estudis Empordanesos speaks of North African pirates under 'Barba-roja'; whether Barbarossa came in person is not settled by these sources

curiosities:A smugglers' village.name: A smugglers' village
curiosities:A smugglers' village.teaser: Cut off by land and close to France, Cadaqués made contraband a trade, then lost its vines in 1879
curiosities:A smugglers' village.story: For most of its history Cadaqués faced the sea because it had no choice: by land there was only a mule track over the Pení. The French border lies just up the coast beyond Portbou, and contraband became a settled trade, landed by boat in coves that had no road. In the 19th century the village grew rich another way, on wine from terraces cut into the schist, until phylloxera reached the Empordà in 1879 and killed the vines. Drive out towards the cape today and the dry-stone terrace walls still step up the bare slopes: a vineyard landscape with no vines left in it.
curiosities:A smugglers' village.why: Look at the empty terraces on the cape road and picture the slopes green with vines.
facts: The abandoned dry-stone terraces on the slopes along the road to Cap de Creus

When the road came: the old guide says both 'the first road in the late 19th century' and 'no easy road until the 20th century', and no source found this week dates the road over the Pení. The 1879 phylloxera date is the old guide's, not re-checked

avoid:August.name: August
avoid:August.teaser: One road in, one month when everyone takes it: August on the GI-614 is a queue, not a drive
avoid:August.story: Cadaqués has one way in by car, the GI-614, a tight mountain road over the Pení from the Roses side. In August the whole coast seems to want the same white village at the same hour. Queues of several kilometres have been recorded, and the narrow schist lanes have nowhere to put the cars, so drivers circle the Riera hunting for a space that is not there. The town that rewards a slow walk turns into a traffic problem with a view. None of this applies in mid-October: this warning is for next summer.
avoid:August.why: Come late May to June or September to October; in August, arrive at first light and walk in.
facts: Nothing to see in October: the road and the parking are back to normal; this is a warning for July and August
Come late May to mid-June or mid-September to October. If it has to be August, drive in at dawn, leave the car in an outer lot and walk; arriving by sea, anchor and take the tender in

avoid:Driving to the lighthouse in summe.name: Driving to the lighthouse in summer
avoid:Driving to the lighthouse in summe.teaser: On restricted summer days the cape road shuts to cars from morning to night: park in town, take the shuttle
avoid:Driving to the lighthouse in summe.story: The road from Cadaqués out to the Cap de Creus lighthouse is narrow and winding, and the cape at its end is the park's most protected ground. So on restricted days in summer it closes to private cars and motorbikes from 9.30am to 9.30pm, watched by cameras, with fines under the municipal ordinance. Drive out anyway and you will be turned back. The park's answer is the shuttle: minibuses from the free Corral d'en Morell car park in town to the lighthouse, with stops on the way, which carry tens of thousands of visitors each summer and keep the cars off the reserve.
avoid:Driving to the lighthouse in summe.why: In season, leave the car at Corral d'en Morell and let the minibus take the bends.
facts: The 2026 restriction is over (it ran on restricted days from June to 31 August). Out of season you can drive to the lighthouse car park, but past calendars also restricted some spring and autumn weekends and December dates: check before setting off

In season, park free at Corral d'en Morell and take the shuttle (tickets online in advance; 2026 fares not verified), or walk the Camí Antic to the cape (its own card). A booking at Restaurant Cap de Creus by the lighthouse may let you drive up: confirm when you book

avoid:A boat day without the forecast.name: A boat day without the forecast
avoid:A boat day without the forecast.teaser: The tramuntana can shut the cape to small boats for days: read the marine forecast the night before
avoid:A boat day without the forecast.story: Cap de Creus is the first land the tramuntana meets as it comes off the Pyrenees, and one of the windiest corners of the Catalan coast. In the season now starting, gusts strong enough to stop small craft are common, and the eastern coves of the cape, so sheltered in the photographs, turn into exposed rock with the sea breaking white over it. Tenders, kayaks and the coastal boat trips simply stay in. A guest promised a cove lunch that cannot happen has a worse day than one planned on land from the start, and the forecast that would have warned you is free and official.
avoid:A boat day without the forecast.why: Check the wind the evening before and again at breakfast, and keep a land plan ready.
facts: Mid-October opens the tramuntana season: on a north-wind day, check the sea state at the cape before any tender, kayak or excursion
Read the Meteocat marine forecast and the Alt Empordà wind warnings the night before (see the Meteocat card) and hold a land plan: the old-town lanes, the Casa-Museu if booked, a long lunch in town

avoid:Portlligat without a slot.name: Portlligat without a slot
avoid:Portlligat without a slot.teaser: Dalí's house lets in small groups at fixed times, booked ahead: walk up without a ticket and you stay outside
avoid:Portlligat without a slot.story: The Casa-Museu at Portlligat is a house, not a gallery: narrow rooms, low passages and stairs between levels, so the foundation lets visitors in a few at a time on a fixed timetable, with every ticket booked in advance. Turn up on spec on a fine day and the slots are usually gone, and the walk over the hill ends at a closed door. Booked tickets must be collected 30 minutes before your time. The house also shuts completely in deep winter, from 7 January to 10 February in the foundation's current calendar, so a January trip built around it fails before it starts.
avoid:Portlligat without a slot.why: Book the house before you book lunch, and be at the door half an hour early.
facts: Open now, booking still required: €15 general online ticket outside summer, €18 in July and August (2025 tariff on the foundation's site, Oct 2026)

follow:Meteocat.name: Meteocat
follow:Meteocat.teaser: The Generalitat's weather service: the forecast every boat day here should start with
follow:Meteocat.story: Meteocat is the Servei Meteorològic de Catalunya, the Generalitat's own weather service, and its forecasts are the ones Catalan civil protection quotes when it puts out wind warnings for the Alt Empordà. For Cadaqués the pages to read are the marine forecast for the Girona coast, with wind direction, strength and sea state, and the warnings map, where a tramuntana episode shows up a day or two ahead. Its network of automatic stations also posts live gusts along the coast. Check it the evening before any boat plan and again at breakfast; the Ports de la Generalitat post harbour notices for the same coast.
follow:Meteocat.why: One look the night before saves a cancelled tender and a stranded lunch.
facts: The Generalitat's weather service: forecasts, warnings and live station data for the Cadaqués coast

follow:Parc Natural de Cap de Creus.name: Parc Natural de Cap de Creus
follow:Parc Natural de Cap de Creus.teaser: The park's own pages: road closures, the shuttle, open trails and the rules in the marine reserve
follow:Parc Natural de Cap de Creus.story: The Generalitat's pages for the Parc Natural de Cap de Creus are the ones to trust on anything that could stop you at the cape: which days the lighthouse road is closed to cars, how the shuttle from Corral d'en Morell works and where to buy tickets online, which trails are open, and what is allowed in the marine reserve and the strictly protected zones. The park was declared in 1998 and takes in land and sea around the whole peninsula. Each season it posts a question-and-answer sheet on the access regulation, with that year's dates and hours.
follow:Parc Natural de Cap de Creus.why: Read the access page before any summer trip to the lighthouse; it changes every year.

follow:Ajuntament de Cadaqués.name: Ajuntament de Cadaqués
follow:Ajuntament de Cadaqués.teaser: Dry reading and the most reliable word in town on the market, the festes, parking and the cape road
follow:Ajuntament de Cadaqués.story: The town hall's own site is plain to look at and the most reliable source for anything practical in Cadaqués. It carries the market and fairs, the festes through the year (Sant Sebastià in January, the summer Festa Major in September, Santa Esperança on 18 December), parking, and a mobility page on the Cap de Creus access regulation, which in 2026 gave the shuttle's dates and running hours. When a feast day, a road rule or the parking changes, this is where it is posted, in Catalan first.
follow:Ajuntament de Cadaqués.why: Check the mobility page before a summer visit and the agenda before planning around a festa.

follow:Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí.name: Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí
follow:Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí.teaser: The foundation Dalí set up himself: Portlligat bookings, and his catalogue of paintings online
follow:Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí.story: The Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí, created by Dalí in 1983, runs his three museums in the Empordà: the house at Portlligat, the Teatre-Museu in Figueres and Gala's castle at Púbol, each with its own card in this guide. Its site is the official booking channel for the Portlligat house, with the timed slots, the rule on collecting tickets and the winter closure. It also hosts the online catalogue raisonné of Dalí's paintings, where you can look up the views of Cadaqués he painted as a boy before you stand on the shore where he set his easel.
follow:Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí.why: Book Portlligat here, then browse the catalogue for the early Cadaqués canvases.

follow:Festival de Música de Cadaqués.name: Festival de Música de Cadaqués
follow:Festival de Música de Cadaqués.teaser: Concerts under Santa Maria's gilded altarpiece every summer since 1970: watch for next year's dates
follow:Festival de Música de Cadaqués.story: The Festival Internacional de Música de Cadaqués has been bringing concerts to the church of Santa Maria since 1970; its story is the music card's. Its season moves: the 52nd edition ran from April to late December 2025, while the 53rd, in 2026, was held between 28 June and 21 August, opening with Handel's Messiah and including Brahms's German Requiem with the Orfeó Gracienc on 24 July. So in October there is nothing to hear. Follow it for the 2027 programme, the venues beyond the church, and the ticket links.
follow:Festival de Música de Cadaqués.why: If a concert night in Santa Maria falls in your window, plan the evening around it.
